entries.title: Ex-Bears kicker Robbie Gould steps down as coach at St. Viator
entries.summary: <p>Less than a week after his second season as St. Viator coach ended, Bears great Robbie Gould has resigned.</p><p>In a release, the school said Gould "made the decision to step away from coaching to spend more time with his family."</p><p>The Lions missed the IHSA playoffs in both of Gould's years in charge, going 2-7 this year and 1-8 in 2025.</p><p>"We are grateful to Coach Gould for his leadership, dedication, and commitment to our student-athletes," St. Viator president Ryan Aiello said in the statement. "We appreciate his contributions to [St.] Viator football, respect his decision to prioritize his family and wish him all the best."</p><p>Gould took over at the Arlington Heights school after one season at Rolling Meadows. The Mustangs went 5-5 and lost to St. Charles North in the first round of the Class 7A playoffs.</p><p>Before moving into high school coaching, Gould played 18 seasons in the NFL — the first 11 with the Bears from 2005-15. He set the franchise career scoring record with 1.961 points and currently ranks 10th in NFL history. After leaving the Bears, he played one season for the Giants and six for the 49ers.</p><p>St. Viator, which plays its home games off campus, has announced plans for an on-campus stadium but the project has faced pushback from neighbors.<br>The school's statement said the search for a new coach has begun.</p>
entries.author: Mike Clark

entries.title: Victims in Mundelein murder-suicide shooting identified
entries.summary: <p>Mundelein police have released the identities of five people killed in an apparent murder-suicide this week.</p><p>Five adults, all related, were found dead after a concerned family member called for a well-being check in the 200 block of Wellington Street around 11:45 p.m. Sunday, Mundelein police said.</p><p>The Lake County Coroner's Office identified the deceased as 80-Year-old James Schmidt, 77-year-old Rebecca Schmidt, 22-year-old Maclaine Schmidt, 37-year-old Nicole Heiser and 51-year-old Bryan Schmidt. </p><p>Bryan Schmidt is believed to be the alleged perpetrator, police said.</p><p>He allegedly shot his four family members before turning the gun on himself, Mundelein police said the preliminary investigation found.</p><p>Multiple suicide notes were left by Bryan Schmidt and found on the scene, police said. The shootings are believed to have taken place between 11 a.m. and 2 p.m. Sunday.</p><p>The family of Heiser, in a statement Wednesday, remembered the woman as a "bright, compassionate soul" who expressed deep love for animals and serving others. </p><p>"We refuse to let her be defined by this horrific violence or simply as a murder victim," the statement said. "Nicole was loyal beyond measure, generous in her time, and an esteemed animal empath — both professionally and within the community. Nicole had a great reverence for the natural world and lived with a sense of stewardship. We are so grateful for our beautiful time together and feel her presence strongly in our precious memories and calm winds."</p><p>Police said they have not had any prior contact with Bryan Schmidt and are working to determine the motive for the shooting.</p><p>Anyone with additional information on the incident is asked to call the Mundelein Police Department at 847-968-4600.</p>
entries.author: Mary Norkol

entries.title: Foundry Park developers break ground on $3 billion project
entries.summary: <p>City and project officials broke ground Wednesday on Foundry Park, the $3 billion megadevelopment that promises to create a new neighborhood along the Chicago River’s North Branch — a vow that the land’s previous owner failed to keep after the pandemic.</p><p>Developer Jim Letchinger and Kayne Anderson Real Estate <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2025/07/10/jdl-kayne-anderson-recalibrate-plans-lincoln-yards-parcel" >acquired</a> the northern chunk of the former Lincoln Yards development site in 2025, after previous owner <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2025/06/27/lincoln-yards-sterling-bay-jdl-development-jim-letchinger-rahm-emanuel" >Sterling Bay</a> couldn’t follow through on its ambitious plans to build towering steel and glass buildings. </p><p>Letchinger’s real estate firm, JDL Development, is breaking ground on something more scaled back: a mixed-income residential development that includes public green space and a 183-room hotel.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure Scott Waguespack (32nd), JDL Development CEO Jim Letchinger, Mayor Brandon Johnson, Kayne Anderson Real Estate Chief Investment Officer David Selznick, Chicago Department of Planning and Development Commissioner Ciere Boatright and Ald. Brian Hopkins (2nd) toss shovels of dirt during the groundbreaking for Foundry Park.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Jim Urquhart/For the Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The groundbreaking comes less than 10 months after JDL and Kayne Anderson notched their <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2026/01/15/foundry-park-deal-gets-clearance-from-chicago-plan-commission" >first city approvals </a>from the Chicago Plan Commission in January — a speed that city officials praised at the groundbreaking on the corner of West Cortland and North Kingsbury streets.</p><p>“We took advantage of what we learned from them,” Letchinger said of Sterling Bay’s attempt at Lincoln Yards. “We go fast, and we had the capital. Capital is critical. We went through planning knowing that as soon as we get this done, we're building.”</p><p>Sterling Bay’s plans for the 53 acres of vacant land called for the equivalent of two Willis Towers’ worth of office space along the Chicago River between Bucktown and Lincoln Park — an amount that outpaced office demand after the COVID-19 pandemic.</p><p>The 31-acre Foundry Park is being built on the northern half of the former Lincoln Yards site and includes the old Finkl Steel property on Cortland Street, along the Chicago River.</p><p>“When I saw an opening to get involved in this incredible piece of land, I jumped at it,” Letchinger said. “Foundry Park offered a blank slate that would allow JDL to create another world-class neighborhood — and there's a lot of them in Chicago. This was an opportunity that we just could not miss.”</p><p>Plans call for more than 3,700 residences, with 20% of them affordable, and 970,000 square feet of office, retail and hotel space. Public parks, riverfront improvements and an extension of The 606 Trail are also planned.</p><p>Renderings show a mix of building heights, with the tallest at roughly 40 stories, grouped near open space and offering riverfront access. In another departure from Lincoln Yards, Foundry Park's buildings will be clad in traditional limestone and brick.</p><p>Phase one will include more than 725 residential units, retail, public green space and underground parking around Southport Avenue and Cortland and Kingsbury streets.</p><p>Letchinger is confident in the future success of Foundry Park because the mix of uses is flexible based on market demand. The homes will include rentals and for-purchase homes. Letchinger knows there’s an opportunity to build even more for-sale homes as <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2026/08/01/cash-properties-sale-open-house-chicago-homebuyers-bidding-wars" >Chicago’s housing market</a> stays hot as inventory thins out.</p><p>“We know what people want,” Letchinger said. “We don't know if we can deliver all of the units right away, but we know over five, six, seven, eight years, the demand will be here. It's actually an unusual project where the more we build, the better it is because it's a neighborhood.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> northern portion of the former Lincoln Yards site.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Jim Urquhart/For the Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Foundry Park will benefit nearby neighborhoods like Logan Square and Lincoln Park as it takes shape, Chicago Department of Planning and Development Commissioner Ciere Boatright said. The development will bring 8 acres of public green space, along with 2,500 jobs.</p><p>When the Cortland and Chicago River tax increment financing district expires in 2043, Foundry Park will be contributing $70 million dollars annually to citywide property taxes, according to Boatright. By 2056, the property will have contributed an estimated $1 billion, making it “one of the most consequential projects in the city's history,” she said.</p><p>The City Council’s Finance Committee approved a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/09/22/foundry-park-mega-project-tif-subsidy-finance-committee-approval" >$201.6 million TIF subsidy</a> for Foundry Park on Sept. 22, nearly a month before developers put shovels in the ground. Much of the funding will be used to redesign and rebuild streets, like Southport and Cortland that for decades, were closed to accommodate companies like Finkl Steel.</p><p>“Foundry Park will be a place where people will want to live, work, visit and raise families and where they can truly call themselves Chicagoans,” Boatright said.</p><p>Mayor Brandon Johnson praised the project for its speed, jobs and mix of uses — though he joked one key element was missing.</p><p>“Looking at the renderings there, Jim, this is impressive,” Johnson said. “Everything is in this site except for our Bears stadium. I know you tried.”</p>
